global.headline: HOUTHI STRIKES ON SAUDI TANKERS SEND OIL PAST $100; HOUSE VOTES AGAIN TO REIN IN TRUMP'S IRAN WAR POWERS
summary: Iran-aligned Houthi rebels claimed missile and drone strikes on two Saudi-flagged oil tankers, Encelia and Layla, in the Red Sea Thursday — setting Encelia ablaze (all crew reported safe) and enforcing the maritime blockade of Saudi ports the group declared earlier in the week. Brent crude surged as much as 6.45% to touch $101.10/barrel, its first close above $100 since May and a roughly 40% gain for the month; Goldman Sachs warned Brent could clear $120 by Q4 if the disruption persists. At least five Saudi crude tankers reversed course in the Red Sea rather than risk transit, adding Bab el-Mandeb to Hormuz as a second chokepoint under direct threat.

In Washington, the House voted 214-208 — with four Republicans (Warren Davidson, Brian Fitzpatrick, Tom Barrett, Thomas Massie) joining Democrats — to direct Trump to end US hostilities against Iran, the second time this war the House has passed such a War Powers resolution (its fifth vote overall); the measure remains symbolic and non-binding. A parallel effort failed hours later in the Senate, where war-critical Republicans again sided with the administration to block debate. CENTCOM completed a 12th consecutive night of strikes (10:30pm ET Wednesday) on Iran's maritime-attack capability, missile/drone storage, coastal surveillance and air-defence sites; Iranian state media reported 2 killed and 11 injured in a missile strike on the Shalamcheh border area.

Separately, New York Times reporting that the Pentagon's official casualty-tracking website understates the American toll reignited a bipartisan transparency dispute, with senators pressing Defence Secretary Hegseth to fully account for troops killed and wounded since his 21 Jul testimony (confirmed 17 dead, war cost $37.5bn). Hegseth has not directly addressed the discrepancy; the true current toll remains unconfirmed pending an authoritative update.
global.geopolitical: Opening a second maritime chokepoint disruption at Bab el-Mandeb, on top of Hormuz, just as a bipartisan House majority formally (if symbolically) votes to curtail the war shows both the conflict's economic footprint and its domestic political cost widening simultaneously, with the administration showing no sign of altering course on either front.
global.socioeconomic: Oil above $100 for the first time since May, layered on an already-tight Hormuz-driven market, directly threatens Singapore's own energy-import costs and shipping/insurance premiums just as households absorb a record Q3 electricity tariff and record COE prices.

global.headline: TRUMP THROWS SAUDI NUCLEAR DEAL INTO DOUBT, DEMANDS ISRAEL RECOGNITION A DAY AFTER SIGNING
summary: A day after his own Energy Secretary signed the landmark US-Saudi civil nuclear cooperation and safeguards agreement (22 Jul), Trump said the pact would take effect only if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords and normalises relations with Israel — a major new condition not mentioned when the deal was inked. Riyadh has long said it will not normalise ties with Israel without a credible pathway to Palestinian statehood, a precondition unmet given Israel's continuing Gaza operations, making the demand a significant practical obstacle to a deal Washington had just finalised.

Analysts described the reversal as characteristic of Trump's dealmaking approach — closing a headline agreement, then attaching fresh leverage — leaving the uranium-enrichment pathway Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman secured (a deal framed as matching Iran's own 440.9kg stockpile enriched to 60%) in limbo pending both Congress's mandatory review and now an entirely new diplomatic precondition.
global.geopolitical: Retroactively tying a signed nuclear-cooperation agreement to Israeli normalisation injects the Gaza/Palestinian-statehood question into a deal that had been framed as a purely energy and security arrangement, testing whether Riyadh will treat US nuclear cooperation as valuable enough to revisit its own long-standing redline.
global.socioeconomic: A stalled, re-conditioned deal delays Saudi Arabia's civil-nuclear diversification away from oil exports at the precise moment Hormuz and now Bab el-Mandeb disruptions are squeezing that same oil revenue, compounding the uncertainty already priced into global energy markets.

global.headline: TRUMP IMPOSES NEW 10-12.5% TARIFFS ON 80+ COUNTRIES AS TEMPORARY GLOBAL LEVY EXPIRES
summary: The Trump administration announced new tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on more than 80 trading partners — including European Union member states, Indonesia and Mexico, together covering an estimated 99.4% of US imports — taking effect at 12:01am Friday (goods already in transit exempted until 4:01am Irish time on 28 Jul). The new duties replace a temporary 10% global tariff imposed under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's original reciprocal-tariff regime in February; officials cited, among other justifications, allegations of lax enforcement of forced-labour import bans among the affected partners.

The move is the White House's latest attempt to restore a near-global tariff framework, and lands as Wall Street was already wobbling Thursday on combined AI-spending and oil-price jitters, with Google and Tesla shares among the sharpest fallers.
global.geopolitical: A tariff reset spanning nearly all US trading partners, arriving the same week Brent tops $100 and the Iran war deepens, doubles down on simultaneous economic and military pressure — testing how much strain on both fronts the administration can sustain before it produces a domestic political reaction.
global.socioeconomic: New double-digit tariffs on the EU and dozens of other partners raise fresh import-cost pressure for trade-dependent economies like Singapore, compounding the Houthi/Hormuz-driven energy-price shock and adding a further variable to MAS's policy calculus.

global.headline: FEDOROV REJECTS ZELENSKY'S ALTERNATIVE OFFERS, WILL ACCEPT NOTHING BUT REINSTATEMENT
summary: Sacked defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Thursday he will accept no role in Zelensky's government other than his old one, turning down an offer to become deputy prime minister for military innovation along with other alternatives floated across several meetings since his 14 Jul dismissal. Fedorov said only the defence-ministry post carries the authority to fight procurement corruption, complete the army's ongoing transformation, run asymmetric operations against Russia, and finish initiatives his team had already started.

The rebuff comes two days before protesters' Friday deadline for Zelensky to reinstate him, and risks reigniting the nationwide demonstrations that followed the sacking, after Zelensky's camp had hoped a face-saving alternative role would defuse the standoff.
global.geopolitical: A wartime president publicly failing to co-opt his own popular, internationally recognised former minister with an alternative post signals the domestic rift runs deeper than a personnel dispute, at a moment Ukraine depends heavily on the drone-warfare and procurement reforms Fedorov built.
global.socioeconomic: Continued uncertainty atop Ukraine's defence-technology and drone-procurement leadership carries direct near-term risk for a military still fighting a materially larger adversary, at a time sustained Western funding confidence depends partly on Kyiv's own institutional stability.

global.headline: INDIA'S WANGCHUK ENDS 26-DAY HUNGER STRIKE AFTER MODI PLEDGES TOUGHER ANTI-PAPER-LEAK LAW
summary: Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike just after midnight Thursday, in the presence of Union Ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh, after PM Modi issued a video address pledging a tougher law against exam-paper leaks and fast-tracked prosecutions of those involved, with the measure now going to Cabinet. Wangchuk had fasted since 28 June in solidarity with the youth-led "Cockroach" movement demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the exam-leak scandals, citing "a long negotiation on various conditions" and concern over "possible violence" in the country as reasons for ending the fast.

The concession is the government's first substantive policy response after days of Bloomberg's "few good options" framing (22 Jul) and a crackdown that injured roughly 180 people (21 Jul) — though it stops short of the Pradhan resignation protesters still camped at Jantar Mantar continue to demand.
global.geopolitical: A direct video pledge from Modi to a hunger-striking activist is a rare public concession from a government that had so far met the youth movement mainly with crackdowns, suggesting Delhi judged the political cost of Wangchuk's health risk as outweighing the cost of a policy concession.
global.socioeconomic: A tougher anti-paper-leak law with fast-tracked prosecutions, if it clears Cabinet, would directly address the structural grievance driving months of unrest among the millions of students competing for scarce exam-gated public-sector and university places.

singapore.headline: GIC'S 20-YEAR REAL RETURN FALLS TO 3.4%, LOWEST IN SIX YEARS, AS FUND PRIORITISES RESILIENCE
summary: GIC's Report on the Management of the Government's Portfolio for 2025/26, released Friday, showed the sovereign wealth fund's rolling 20-year annualised real rate of return — its primary performance benchmark — fell to 3.4%, down from 3.8% a year earlier and the lowest since FY2019/20's 2.7%; the unadjusted 20-year annualised nominal return was 5.6%. GIC's portfolio is estimated at roughly US$930 billion.

GIC said it had prioritised resilience through diversification and took less risk this year, moderating returns in exchange for greater downside protection and flexibility to act on opportunities as they emerge — language consistent with CEO Lim Chow Kiat's prior framing of a world facing cyclical, structural and foundational shifts, including fragmentation of the global trading system and AI's economic impact.
singapore.geopolitical: A third consecutive year of declining 20-year real returns, delivered through a deliberately lower-risk posture, signals Singapore's own sovereign fund reading current global conditions — an active Iran war, a fresh global tariff reset, AI-spending volatility — as meriting caution over return-maximisation.
singapore.socioeconomic: A lower long-run real return on Singapore's reserves carries direct fiscal relevance given the Net Investment Returns Contribution's role funding the Budget, at a time record COE prices, electricity tariffs and GST Voucher payouts already strain the government's cost-of-living balancing act.

singapore.headline: EX-IRAS TAX INVESTIGATOR, DIRECTOR CHARGED OVER ILLICIT ACCESS TO TAXPAYER DATA FOR FRIENDS
summary: Mansur @ Thio Shuang Long, 49, a former IRAS Principal Tax Investigator, and Loh Chee Wee, 50, a director of Transstar Asia Pte Ltd, were charged in court under the Computer Misuse and Cybersecurity Act and the Official Secrets Act, CPIB said. Between May 2014 and January 2016, Mansur allegedly used his IRAS access to obtain taxpayer information in response to queries from friends and acquaintances, including telling Loh in July 2014 whether a company sharing office space with Transstar Asia was under IRAS investigation.

Neither man indicated a plea; both cases were adjourned to 19 August. The charges resolve a story first flagged via bare Straits Times/Mothership headlines on 22 Jul that could not be independently corroborated at the time.
singapore.geopolitical: Prosecuting a decade-old internal tax-data leak under the Official Secrets Act signals how seriously Singapore treats breaches of confidential taxpayer information even years after the fact, a message aimed at sustaining trust in IRAS's systems among foreign investors and treaty partners as much as domestic taxpayers.
singapore.socioeconomic: The case is a reminder that Singapore's reputation for tight, trustworthy tax administration — a pillar of its business-hub status — rests on individual compliance as much as on the underlying legal framework, with real custodial risk for insiders who breach it.

singapore.headline: NAVY LAUNCHES SECOND MULTI-ROLE COMBAT VESSEL, VALOUR, AT ST ENGINEERING'S BENOI SHIPYARD
summary: Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs K Shanmugam officiated the launch of the Republic of Singapore Navy's second Victory-class Multi-Role Combat Vessel, Valour, at ST Engineering's Benoi Shipyard Thursday. Valour now moves into outfitting, combat-systems integration and acceptance trials, with its pioneer crew beginning training; MINDEF says the six-ship class, ordered under a 2023 contract, will be delivered progressively from 2028.
The MRCVs are designed as hybrid frigates and drone motherships intended to project Singapore naval power further, and for longer, than earlier vessel classes.
singapore.geopolitical: Progressing a six-ship next-generation frigate/drone-mothership programme on schedule, even as the minister overseeing it takes on the new Senior Minister role from 27 Jul, underscores continuity in Singapore's long-term naval modernisation regardless of the Cabinet reshuffle happening around it.
singapore.socioeconomic: A drone-mothership-capable frigate class reflects Singapore's bet that unmanned and autonomous maritime systems, not just traditional hulls, will define regional naval power projection over the vessels' multi-decade service life — a capability investment that also anchors high-value shipbuilding and systems-integration work at home via ST Engineering.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE REAFFIRMS PALESTINIAN AUTHORITY SUPPORT, MEETS UNRWA CHIEF AT MANILA ASEAN MEETINGS
summary: Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan reaffirmed Singapore's support for Palestinian Authority capacity-building at the Conference on Cooperation Among East Asian Countries for Palestinian Development, held alongside the 59th ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Manila. He pointed to Singapore's S$10 million Enhanced Technical Assistance Package — training, study visits and scholarships for Palestinians — and separately met UNRWA Commissioner-General Christian Saunders to discuss the agency's humanitarian role.
Singapore has contributed roughly 11 tranches of humanitarian assistance worth US$19 million to Gaza since October 2023, per MFA.
singapore.geopolitical: Reaffirming Palestinian Authority support and engaging UNRWA directly, even as Trump's Saudi nuclear deal now explicitly ties US-Saudi nuclear cooperation to Israel normalisation, positions Singapore's stated two-state-solution stance against a moment when a major regional power is under fresh US pressure to move the opposite way.
singapore.socioeconomic: The Enhanced Technical Assistance Package's capacity-building focus, rather than direct budget support, reflects Singapore's standard aid model of technical training over cash transfers — a lower-cost way to sustain its stated Palestinian-development commitment within a modest S$10 million envelope.

word.definition: In diplomacy, the practice of deliberately tying progress on one agreement or issue to concessions on an unrelated matter, using the first as leverage to extract movement on the second.
word.etymology: From Middle English linke ("ring of a chain"), ultimately from Old Norse hlenkr; the abstract diplomatic sense of tying unrelated negotiations together as leverage was popularised by Henry Kissinger's US-Soviet arms-control strategy in the early 1970s.
word.example: A day after signing it, Trump imposed a fresh act of linkage on the US-Saudi nuclear deal, declaring it would take effect only once Riyadh joined the Abraham Accords and normalised ties with Israel.
